article.title: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid Reaches General Availability With Pricing Still Unpublished
article.summary: Microsoft's on-premises extension of Azure Virtual Desktop is now GA, using Azure Arc to broker desktops hosted on customer hardware, but service pricing remains undisclosed.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Microsoft has made Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid generally available, according to [Microsoft's official Azure Virtual Desktop changelog](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-desktop/whats-new), which confirms the service "is now generally available" and "extends Azure Virtual Desktop to existing on-premises infrastructure, enabling organizations to run session hosts on on-premises hypervisors or physical Windows Server devices." The move lets organizations keep desktop virtualization workloads on their own hardware while Microsoft continues to host and manage the brokering service in Azure, as [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/) reported.

## What We Know

Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid uses Azure Arc to bridge on-premises infrastructure with the cloud-hosted control plane. Per [Microsoft's architecture documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-desktop/hybrid-overview), the deployment flow works in four steps: an organization deploys a Windows virtual machine or headless physical device on-premises, installs the Azure Arc connected machine agent to register it as an Arc-enabled server, runs the Azure Virtual Desktop Arc extension to install the AVD software and register the machine with the service, and users then connect "using Windows App, the same way they connect to any Azure Virtual Desktop session host."

Under this model, Microsoft "manages the Azure Virtual Desktop service in Azure," while the customer "manage[s] the on-premises machines, networking, and hosting infrastructure," according to the documentation. According to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/), the service maintains the same architecture that Microsoft introduced during a limited preview in November 2025, with all communication traveling outbound over HTTPS, eliminating inbound connectivity requirements.

Operating system support is narrower than standard Azure Virtual Desktop. Microsoft's documentation lists Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025 as supported when licensed through Remote Desktop Services Client Access Licenses with Software Assurance, running on "virtual machines and headless physical servers." Windows 11 Enterprise and Windows 10 Enterprise are also supported, but only in single-session form and only "on virtual machines," with physical devices restricted to "dedicated, headless session hosts (rack-mounted or similar)" — the documentation specifies that "laptops and personal PCs aren't supported." Windows 11 and Windows 10 Enterprise multi-session are explicitly listed as "Not Supported" on Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid.

That multi-session gap has practical cost implications: [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/) noted that "multi-session deployments typically support two to six users per vCPU depending on workload; single-session requires dedicated VM allocation per user," substantially increasing the compute organizations need to provision on-premises.

Microsoft's documentation also states that Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid "doesn't provision or manage virtual machine state," meaning power management, autoscale, Start VM on Connect, and session host configuration are all unsupported — organizations must handle those tasks themselves "using hypervisor tools, scripts, partner solutions, or other tools." Session hosts still require outbound access to login.microsoftonline.com and *.wvd.microsoft.com endpoints for authentication and RDP connectivity, per [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/).

On pricing, [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/) reported that organizations need OS user licensing plus "a separate Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid service license," but that "Microsoft has not yet published pricing details for the service component, creating uncertainty among potential adopters."

## Reactions

Feedback from partners who tested the service during preview points to the Software Assurance requirement as a significant adoption barrier. [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/avd-hybrid-ga/) reported that one Microsoft MVP said the requirement "kills around 90% of our potential customer deployments" since most customers lack Software Assurance or bought licenses without it. Multiple preview participants also asked for Windows 11 multi-session support, with one telling Microsoft: "Good move. I could onboard more customers with this. Even more if you added win11 multi."

## What We Don't Know

Microsoft has not disclosed pricing for the Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid service license, leaving organizations unable to fully budget for adoption. No specific general-availability date within September 2026 has been published beyond the month itself. It also remains unclear whether or when Microsoft might extend support to Windows 11 or Windows 10 Enterprise multi-session, despite preview-tester requests for it.

## Why It Matters

The use case Microsoft is targeting is regulated or data-residency-sensitive workloads: keeping session hosts and application data on-premises while Azure hosts the control plane, satisfying compliance requirements that a fully cloud-hosted desktop cannot meet. Whether that use case gains traction now depends heavily on licensing terms Microsoft has yet to publish.
